new_statements.quote: In de woorden van Aghu, Kaeti, Wambon, en in Kati I en II valt de klemtoon op de laatste lettergreep; in samengestelde woorden kan dat anders zijn, en we geven de klemtoon dan aan met een accent grave, zoals we ook doen in de dialecten Sjiagha, Jénimu en ... [p.12:] ... samenstelling van het Germaanse type „boomstam", die men vindt in alle bekende Papoea-talen, met de klemtoon op het eerste, het bepalende gedeelte; daar echter in deze taal elk woord de klemtoon heeft op de laatste lettergr. is dat in gevallen als in onze tekst vaak niet goed te horen; voorbeelden van deze samenstelling zijn: mbüman-mirap ruggegraat, ndüàm-wegi bamboemes ...
new_statements.translation: In the words of Aghu, Kaeti, Wambon, and in Kati I and II the stress falls on the last syllable; in compound words it can be otherwise, and we then mark the stress with a grave accent, as we also do in the dialects Sjiagha, Jenimu and ... [p.12:] ... compounding of the Germanic 'tree-trunk' type, found in all known Papuan languages, with the stress on the first, modifying part; but since in this language every word has the stress on the last syllable, in cases like those in our text this is often hard to hear; examples of this compounding are: mbüman-mirap 'backbone', ndüàm-wegi 'bamboo knife' ...

The dc:description snippets contain, verbatim modulo the feed's tokenised spacing: (q3/q6) '.. zwak accent valt op de eerste der twee. De halfklinkers, voorkomende in tweeklanken, schrijven we e, i enz. In de woorden van Aghu, Kaeti, Wambon, en in Kati I en II valt de klemtoon op de laatste lettergreep; in samengestelde..'; (q10/q17) '.. valt de klemtoon op de laatste lettergreep; in samengestelde…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (klemtoon) in Kaeti (= Mandobo, Drabbe's Rungwanjap variety) falls on the final syllable of every non-compound word; Drabbe leaves it unmarked and writes a grave accent only where stress is non-final, which happens in compounds (modifier-stressed 'boomstam' compounds; coordinate compounds with both members stressed).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. (Separately Drabbe notes a 'zwak accent' on the first of two vowels in hiatus ('dubbele klanken'), a vowel-sequence remark, not a secondary-stress rule.)
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds: stress may fall elsewhere ('in samengestelde woorden kan dat anders zijn'), marked with a grave; a further snippet says any case where stress falls on other than the last syllable will be marked ('klemtoon op een andere dan de laatste lettergr. valt, zullen we dat [aangeven]'). No lexical exceptions listed in the text seen.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('elk woord de klemtoon heeft op de laatste lettergreep'); statement is a blanket one covering all Aghu, Kaeti, Wambon and Kati forms cited in the book; compounds treated separately. Only snippet-length context seen; full paragraph and exact page not verified on a scan.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is Drabbe's (1959) for 'Kaeti' (= Mandobo), specifically the Rungwanjap dialect of the middle Dumut/Mandobo River (informant from the Omba clan on the Marek tributary; Wester 2014:7). Glottolog attaches Drabbe 1959 to Mandobo Atas [aax] mand1444 and Mandobo Bawah [bwp] mand1445, NOT to Kokenop Mandobo [koke1241], which Glottolog split off precisely because Jang (2003:20-25) found the speech of Kokenop, Bukit, Kogonop and Agayop unintelligible with Winiktit and other Mandobo Atas villages. No phonological description of Kokenop Mandobo itself exists (only Stokhof 1982 Holle list 230d, c.50 words, and Jang 2003's unpublished survey wordlists). The same Drabbe sentence also asserts final stress for Aghu [aghu1255], for his Wambon (= Yonggom Wambon of van den Heuvel 2025; final stress confirmed there p.19) and for Kati I/II (= Muyu, Ok family). Recommendation: catalog this quote under mand1444/mand1445 (both currently the named source could not be reached), and treat koke1241 as undescribed, at most inheriting 'final stress' as a Dumut-cluster expectation (note Digul Wambon in the same cluster is penultimate per de Vries & de Vries-Wiersma 1992, so cluster inference is not safe).

new_statements.quote: [Wambon, p.379:] The phonemes in Wambon are: p ... i, e, a, o, u. Suprasegmentals: weak stress on the final syllable of monomorphemic words; otherwise no rules of stress placement have been given. [Kaeti, p.380:] Drabbe (1959d) published texts with explanatory notes in Kaeti. The sound system of Kaeti is similar to the sound system of Wambon; it lacks a velar nasal (ŋ), and has two additional vowel phonemes, ü and ö. It is difficult to get a clear picture of the grammatical structure of Kaeti from Drabbe's notes. It seems that it is very similar to the grammatical structure of Wambon, so much so that one would expect Kaeti to be a dialect of Wambon rather than a separate language.

A grammatical sketch.. has been published by Drabbe (1959d). The phonemes in Wambon are: p.. i, e, a, o, u. Reading fixed: final syllable / stress correct. IDENTITY CORRECTIO…
new_statements.relation_note: Elsewhere in the same chapter Voorhoeve gives per-language suprasegmental notes for Awyu languages (e.g. Aghu-type 'weak stress on the last syllable of monomorphemic words', p.378) and Kati (final stress, compounds stress last syllable of first constituent, p.382) -- all outside this key.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Drabbe's Wambon (upper Mandobo River): weak stress on the final syllable of monomorphemic words (second-hand from Drabbe 1959). For Kaeti (= Mandobo proper) only 'sound system similar to Wambon' -- no explicit stress statement; Voorhoeve declines to survey Kaeti separately.
new_statements.exceptions: 'otherwise no rules of stress placement have been given' (i.e. polymorphemic words/compounds not covered)
new_statements.identity_note: Sec.2.6.2.2.6.2.7 'Kaeti' (p.380): 'spoken by approximately 4,000 people living in the basin of the Mandobo River. There are two dialects, Kambom on the lower Mandobo and Runggwanyap on the middle Mandobo' = Glottolog Mandobo Bawah mand1445 / Mandobo Atas mand1444 (Drabbe's Kaeti); sec.2.6.2.2.6.2.6 'Wambon' (p.379) = Drabbe's Wambon of the Mandobo headwaters (= Yonggom Wambon of van den Heuvel 2025). Kokenop/Bukit villages are not mentioned; all information is second-hand from Drabbe 1959. | Our bibliography files this book as a sister-lect source ('Drabbe's Wambon.. Nothing specific on Kaeti/Mandobo stress') and A repeated that. The variety is Drabbe's 1959 Wambon, whose 'language helpers lived' at Waniktit (= Winiktit, upper Kao; book pp.4-7, Figure 5 marks 'Winiktit = Waniktit') and whose speech community Drabbe (1959:115, translated p.6) defines as the self-designated Wambon of six villages 'Waniktit, Jumgubub, Anumjandit, Maramsan (new place Mirapjandit), Ukjandit and Wombon', c.1,000 people near Mount Koreom -- explicitly 'not those who are called Wambon by the Kaeti's'. In Jang 2003's classification (reproduced in Gusmao 2024 Table 1) Wombon village = 'Agayop' inside 'Kokenop Mandobo' and Winiktit = 'Mandobo-Wambon' inside 'Upper Mandobo'; Glottolog 5.3 follows this exactly: Agayop agay1235 is one of koke1241's three dialects, Winiktit wini1246 sits under Mandobo Atas mand1444. Usher (Newguineaworld) labels Drabbe's Waniktit Wambon 'Agayop' and pairs it with Kokenop as 'East Wambon (= Yonggom Wambon)'; Jang 2003:26 (via Usher) has Wombon villagers stating their dialect is identical to Winiktit's; Gusmao 2024 finds Winiktit, Wombon, Wariktop, Tetop speakers all call their lect Agayop and that Bukit-Kokenop and Winiktit-Agayop speakers understand each other fully. Hence this is a first-hand-based description of the Agayop lect of the Kokenop/Agayop cluster -- 'probably' rather than 'yes' only because Glottolog keys the informants' village Winiktit to mand1444. It is NOT Digul Wambon wamb1259 [wms] (Glottolog's 'Wambon' = Kenondik/Kenyam/Kawagit + Upper Wambon; penultimate stress per de Vries), despite our catalogue tree storing the text under wamb1259. | Same book as the existing statement, but the OTHER half: the existing statement quotes the Kaeti (Rungwanjap Mandobo, mand1444/mand1445) Klankleer; this is the Wambon Klankleer, i.e. the Waniktit/Wombon ('Agayop') lect discussed under missed work 1 -- Wombon = Glottolog agay1235 under koke1241, Waniktit = wini1246 under mand1444. A saw this snippet ('one further snippet.. the Wambon Klankleer') but treated it as the existing work re-served and as a sister lect, so did not list or key it.

new_statements.quote: [p.6, Drabbe 1959:115 in translation:] In the North, close to the Koreom, we find people who call themselves Wambon; they live in six villages: Waniktit, Jumgubub, Anumjandit, Maramsan (new place Mirapjandit), Ukjandit and Wombon (not Wambon!), and number around 1,000 people. Note that the Wambon people whose dialect we describe here are not those who are called Wambon by the Kaeti's [speakers of Mandobo], who speak a subdialect of Mandobo. ... [p.19:] 1.2.3 Lexical stress. In all non-compound words, and in all verbs, stress is on the last syllable of the word. Drabbe speaks of a 'weak accent'. Because lexical stress is predictable, it is not indicated in spelling. For stress in compounds, see Chapter 3, Section 3.1.1. ... [p.91:] According to Drabbe, Yonggom Wambon (YW) has two types of compounds: those in which both nouns keep their own lexical stress, and those in which stress is on one of the two composing parts. ... [p.92:] In both subtypes, the main stress is on the modifying noun. In the examples discussed below, stress is indicated by an accent grave. ... [p.224:] In all non-compound words, stress is on the last syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (Drabbe's 'zwakke klemtoon', weak accent) falls on the final syllable of every non-compound word and of every verb form; it is predictable and therefore unmarked; the domain is the phonological word (sec.1.5).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. Compounds: exocentric (coordinate) compounds keep stress on both members; compounds with linker o carry main stress on the o; endocentric compounds carry main stress on the modifying noun (marked with a grave in Drabbe's spelling).
new_statements.exceptions: Only compounds (secs 3.1.1.1-3.1.1.2); no lexical exceptions listed.
